claims.text: The feedstock is a cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi high-entropy alloy powder.
The proposed intervention is in-situ powder-bed or substrate preheating during LPBF.
LPBF should be conducted in a controlled inert atmosphere.
Laser scanning parameters should be adjusted to account for the elevated base temperature.
Preheating to 500–600 °C reduces thermal gradients across the melt pool and layer interfaces.
Higher substrate temperature lowers the quenching rate during solidification.
Lower quenching rates and reduced thermal gradients minimize compositional segregation at solidification fronts.
Reduced thermal gradients lower residual stresses induced by steep temperature differentials.
Preheating produces a more uniform microstructure with fewer processing-induced defects.
Preheated LPBF parts will have greater tensile strength than non-preheated LPBF controls.
Preheated LPBF parts will have greater ductility than non-preheated LPBF controls.
Preheated LPBF parts will have lower residual stress than non-preheated LPBF controls.
Preheated LPBF parts will exhibit less compositional segregation than non-preheated LPBF controls.
Conventional LPBF without substrate preheating typically produces significant thermal gradients, segregation, high residual stresses, and increased defect formation in AlCrFeNiSi.
The hypothesis is valid within a 500–600 °C preheating range under an inert atmosphere.
Excessive preheating or an unsuitable scan speed may cause grain coarsening or phase instability.
The intervention can be tested by comparing preheated and room-temperature-substrate LPBF samples using tensile tests, residual-stress mapping, segregation analysis, and defect imaging.
